hypothesis: Triple‐negative breast cancers (ER–, PR–, HER2–) exhibit higher expression of basal marker KRT5 compared to non‐triple‐negative cancers.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Compare KRT5 expression between TNBC and non‐TNBC patients, with a fallback to a composite basal cytokeratin signature if KRT5 is missing in the dataset.

Steps: 1. Load clinical metadata (cleaned_clinical_data.csv) and select columns: bcr_patient_barcode, er_status, pr_status, her2_ihc_status.  Define TNBC label as er_status=='Negative' AND pr_status=='Negative' AND her2_ihc_status=='Negative'.

2. Load gene expression matrix (cleaned_gene_expression.csv) using the first column as row index (Ensembl gene IDs with version suffix) and the remaining columns as patient barcodes.

3. Attempt to locate the Ensembl ID for KRT5:
   a. Remove version suffix from all row indices (split at the first dot) and look for the prefix 'ENSG00000134305'.
   b. If one or more matches are found, select the row that has non‐zero variance across samples (to avoid pseudogene rows) and designate it as the KRT5 expression vector.

4. If no match for KRT5 is found in step 3:
   a. Define a small list of basal cytokeratin Ensembl IDs (without version suffix) that are likely present in the data, for example: KRT14 (ENSG00000168638), KRT17 (ENSG00000000000 – replace with correct), KRT6A (ENSG00000198888), etc.
   b. For each of these IDs, scan the index in the same way (split and match prefix).  Keep only those genes found in the dataset.
   c. Compute a composite basal signature for each patient as the row‐wise mean expression across all found basal genes.
   d. Use this composite signature in place of KRT5.

5. Create a table with patient barcodes, TNBC label, and the chosen expression vector (KRT5 or composite basal signature).

6. Generate summary statistics of the expression by group:
   - Mean, median, and interquartile range (IQR) for TNBC and non‐TNBC.

7. Visualize the distributions using a boxplot (two boxes side by side: TNBC vs non‐TNBC).

8. Perform a statistical test for difference in medians: use a Wilcoxon rank‐sum test (Mann‐Whitney U).  Also report a two‐sample t‐test if normality appears plausible.

9. Record and report: group sample sizes; summary statistics; test statistic and p‐value; interpretation (e.g., whether TNBC shows significantly higher basal marker expression).

10. Document whether the analysis used KRT5 directly or a composite signature due to missing KRT5.


Deliverables: • A table showing TNBC vs non‐TNBC sample counts and summary statistics (mean, median, IQR) of KRT5 or composite basal signature.
• A boxplot comparing expression levels between groups.
• Wilcoxon rank‐sum test statistic and p‐value (and optionally two‐sample t‐test results).
• A brief note on whether KRT5 was directly measured or a composite signature was used due to dataset limitations.
analysis:
The code successfully executed a fallback analysis using a composite basal keratin signature (KRT14, KRT6A, KRT17) because KRT5 was not found. 

• Marker used: Composite basal signature (mean of KRT14, KRT6A, KRT17)
• Sample sizes: TNBC=113, Non-TNBC=955

Summary of expression (log2 FPKM):
 - TNBC: mean=11.370, median=11.177, IQR=1.364
 - Non-TNBC: mean=11.769, median=11.769, IQR=1.066

Statistical tests:
 - Wilcoxon rank-sum: U=39663.0, p<0.0001
 - Two-sample t-test: t=–4.483, p<0.0001

Interpretation: Contrary to the original hypothesis, Non-TNBC tumors exhibited significantly higher basal keratin signature expression than TNBC (p≪0.001).
review: The experiment was adjusted to handle missing KRT5 expression by using a composite basal keratin signature (KRT14, KRT6A, KRT17). The analysis merged clinical TNBC labels with the composite signature, provided summary statistics, performed appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon rank-sum and t-test), and reported results and a boxplot. The implementation faithfully follows the revised experiment plan and tests the hypothesis (in its adapted form). Findings indicate Non-TNBC tumors have significantly higher basal signature expression than TNBC (p < 0.0001), contrary to the original hypothesis.

review:

review:

- Clinical data loaded and filtered for complete neoadjuvant_treatment, tumor_status, and receptor status.

hypothesis: Patients with positive or close surgical margins have shorter disease-free survival than those with negative margins.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Robustly evaluate the association between surgical margin status and disease-free survival, ensuring adequate sample size for Cox modeling and meeting assumption checks.

Steps: 1. Load ‘cleaned_clinical_data.csv’ into a DataFrame.
2. Retain all patients with non-missing ‘surgical_margin’ and with at least one follow-up time: use ‘days_to_new_tumor’ when a new tumor event is recorded (‘YES’), otherwise treat missing ‘new_tumor_event’ or ‘NO’ as censored at ‘days_to_last_followup’.  
3. Recode surgical margins into two groups: Negative vs. Positive/Close.  
4. For each patient define:  
   • time = days_to_new_tumor if new_tumor_event==’YES’, else days_to_last_followup  
   • event = 1 if new_tumor_event==’YES’, else 0  
5. Check group counts; ensure each margin group has sufficient sample size (e.g., >50 patients per group). If Positive/Close still too small (<20), report counts and limit further modeling to univariate.  
6. Kaplan–Meier analysis:  
   • Fit and plot survival curves for Negative vs Positive/Close.  
   • Conduct log-rank test and report p-value.  
7. Cox proportional hazards regression:  
   a. Univariate model: margin_group as predictor.  
   b. Multivariable model: adjust for age_at_diagnosis and a simplified pathologic_stage (collapse into Stage I–II vs III–IV).  
   c. To ensure convergence and reduce collinearity, apply an L2 penalizer (e.g., penalizer=0.1).  
8. Extract hazard ratios (HR), 95% confidence intervals, and p-values for margin_group and covariates.  
9. Check proportional hazards assumptions (e.g., Schoenfeld residuals) for key variables; if violated, report results stratified or include time‐interaction term.  

Deliverables:
• Table of group sample sizes and median disease-free survival times for each margin group.  
• Kaplan–Meier plot with confidence intervals and log-rank p-value.  
• Cox regression summaries: univariate and multivariable models with HRs, CIs, and p-values.  
• Diagnostics on proportional hazards assumptions (test statistics, plots or summary).  
• Narrative interpretation of whether positive/close margins confer significantly shorter disease-free survival.

Deliverables: 1. Summary table: counts and median survival by margin group.  
2. Kaplan–Meier survival plot with log-rank test annotation.  
3. Univariate and multivariable Cox model output (HRs, 95% CIs, p-values).  
4. PH assumption diagnostics report.  
5. Written interpretation of findings regarding the impact of surgical margins on disease-free survival.
analysis:
The revised analysis met all deliverables with adequate group sizes (Negative n=866, Positive/Close n=96).

hypothesis: Patients receiving postoperative pharmaceutical therapy exhibit distinct gene co-expression network modules enriched for chemotherapy metabolism pathways compared to untreated patients.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Use a full WGCNA‐style pipeline to identify gene co‐expression modules in breast cancer RNA-Seq data and test their associations with postoperative pharmaceutical therapy while adjusting for age and pathologic stage, then perform pathway enrichment on significant modules focusing on drug metabolism.

Steps: 1. Load the two data files:
   • cleaned_gene_expression.csv (log2(FPKM+0.001) for ~60k genes × 1068 samples)
   • cleaned_clinical_data.csv (clinical metadata for 1097 patients)
   Align sample IDs by truncating expression column names to the first 12 characters to match bcr_patient_barcode.

2. Define analysis cohort:
   • Retain only samples where pharmaceutical_therapy is “YES” or “NO”.
   • Create a binary treatment vector (1=YES, 0=NO).
   • Extract age_at_diagnosis (numeric) and pathologic_stage (e.g., Stage I, IIA, IIB, IIIA, IIIB, IV); encode stage as dummy variables or ordinal numeric values.

3. Gene filtering:
   • Compute variance of each gene across retained samples.
   • Select the top 5,000 most variable genes to reduce noise and computation.

4. Soft‐threshold power selection:
   • For a range of candidate powers (e.g., 1–20), compute the adjacency matrix for each power using adjacency_ij = |cor(cori,j)|^power.
   • For each power, calculate the scale‐free topology fit index and mean connectivity.
   • Choose the smallest power that achieves a scale‐free fit index ≥0.85 (or the inflection point in the fit vs power curve) while maintaining adequate mean connectivity.

5. Adjacency and TOM calculation:
   • Using the chosen power, compute the adjacency matrix.
   • Convert adjacency to the topological overlap matrix (TOM) and derive TOM‐based dissimilarity (1 – TOM).

6. Module detection:
   • Perform hierarchical clustering on genes using TOM dissimilarity.
   • Apply dynamic tree cut (minModuleSize=30) to define initial modules and merge modules with eigengene correlation >0.75 (mergeCutHeight=0.25).

7. Module eigengenes:
   • For each module, calculate the module eigengene (first principal component of the scaled expression matrix of its genes).
   • Assemble an eigengene matrix (samples × modules).

8. Association testing:
   • For each module eigengene, fit a linear model: eigengene ~ treatment + age_at_diagnosis + (stage dummy variables).
   • Extract the coefficient, t‐statistic, and p‐value for the treatment term.
   • Adjust module p‐values for multiple testing using the Benjamini‐Hochberg procedure (FDR).

9. Identify significant modules:
   • Select modules with treatment‐term FDR < 0.05.

10. Pathway enrichment:
   • For each significant module, take its gene list and perform pathway enrichment (e.g., via Enrichr or similar) against the KEGG_2019_Human gene sets.
   • Filter enrichment results for drug metabolism and related pathways (e.g., “Drug metabolism – cytochrome P450”, “ABC transporters”, “Glutathione metabolism”).

11. Visualization and reporting:
   • Plot scale‐free topology fit vs power curve and mean connectivity vs power curve.
   • Plot the gene dendrogram colored by final module assignments.
   • Produce a module‐trait heatmap showing the correlation between module eigengenes and treatment, age, and stage (with p‐values).
   • For each significant module, present the KEGG drug metabolism enrichment bar plot.


Deliverables: 1. A plot of scale‐free topology fit index and mean connectivity across candidate powers, with chosen power annotated.
2. A table of gene‐to‐module assignments for the 5,000 filtered genes.
3. A matrix of module eigengenes (samples × modules) and their corresponding clinical covariates.
4. A results table for each module: module ID, number of genes, treatment effect estimate, t‐statistic, p‐value, FDR.
5. A module‐trait heatmap showing correlations and p‐values for treatment, age, and stage.
6. For each module with FDR < 0.05, a table of KEGG enrichment results filtered for drug metabolism pathways (Term, overlap, adjusted p‐value), plus corresponding bar plots.
7. Gene dendrogram with dynamic tree cut modules and merged module color annotations.
analysis: The pipeline completed successfully. 5,000 top variable genes were clustered into 9 modules, module eigengenes were computed, and linear models (adjusting for age and stage) tested treatment effects. Two modules had nominal p < 0.05 but none passed FDR < 0.05, so no pathway enrichment was performed. All deliverables—inclusive of power selection plot, module definitions, eigengene–trait tests, and visualizations—were generated.
review:
Hypothesis: Patients receiving postoperative pharmaceutical therapy may harbor distinct gene co-expression modules enriched for drug metabolism pathways.

The revised pipeline now implements a full WGCNA-inspired workflow: 
– Filtered to 5,000 most variable genes.
– Selected soft-threshold power based on scale-free fit and mean connectivity.
– Computed adjacency and TOM, performed hierarchical clustering, and applied dynamic tree cut (via cutreeHybrid) with subsequent module merging (eigengene correlation >0.75). Final network yielded 9 modules (sizes 39–1883 genes).
– Calculated module eigengenes and tested their association with treatment status in linear models adjusting for age and pathologic stage. Two modules showed nominal significance (p<0.05), but none remained significant after FDR correction (smallest FDR=0.167).
– No modules met FDR < 0.05, so no drug metabolism pathway enrichment was detected.

All specified deliverables were produced: scale-free topology plots; gene-to-module assignments; module eigengene–trait association table including FDR; module–trait heatmap; and gene dendrogram with module colors. The negative result indicates no pharmaceutical therapy–associated modules at FDR < 0.05.

hypothesis: High expression of a proliferation gene signature (MKI67, PCNA, TOP2A) predicts shorter time to new tumor event after initial treatment, controlling for treatment and pathologic stage.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Compute a per-patient proliferation signature score and assess its association with recurrence-free survival (time to new tumor event), ensuring correct mapping between expression samples and clinical patient barcodes.

Steps: 1. Load clinical table (cleaned_clinical_data.csv) and gene expression matrix (cleaned_gene_expression.csv).  
2. Extract the set of clinical patient barcodes (column bcr_patient_barcode).  
3. Process gene expression column names: for each sample header, split on '-' and reassemble the first three fields (e.g. TCGA-XX-YYYY), which corresponds to the patient-level barcode.  
4. Compare processed expression IDs to clinical barcodes; report the number of overlapping IDs and list any mismatches.  
5. Rename gene expression columns to the patient-level barcodes for the overlapping set, and subset the expression matrix to these matched patients.  
6. Preprocess gene expression rows: strip version suffix from Ensembl IDs (split on '.'), so that base IDs match mapping.  
7. Map proliferation signature gene symbols to their Ensembl IDs (e.g. MKI67→ENSG00000148773, PCNA→ENSG00000153029, TOP2A→ENSG00000131747); verify that each Ensembl ID is present after stripping versions.  
8. Extract expression values for the three signature genes and rename rows to gene symbols.  
9. For each gene, compute its patient-wise z-score (subtract mean and divide by standard deviation across patients), then average the three z-scores to yield a per-patient proliferation_score.  
10. Construct recurrence data from clinical: define time = days_to_new_tumor if new_tumor_event='YES', else days_to_last_followup; define event indicator = 1 if new_tumor_event='YES', else 0; drop patients with missing time or event.  
11. Merge proliferation_score into the clinical recurrence table by patient.  
12. Recode covariates: neoadjuvant_treatment and pharmaceutical_therapy into binary indicators; one-hot encode pathologic_stage (drop first category).  
13. Before model fitting, verify that merged dataset has at least 20 patients and at least 5 events; if not, document and consider merging similar stages or relaxing filters.  
14. Fit a Cox proportional hazards model: Surv(time, event) ~ proliferation_score + neoadjuvant + pharmaceutical + pathologic_stage_dummies.  
15. Validate model: check for missing values and drop any remaining NaNs; test proportional hazards assumptions (e.g. Schoenfeld residuals).  
16. Report the hazard ratio (exp(coef)), 95% confidence interval, and p-value for proliferation_score.  
17. Dichotomize proliferation_score at its median into High vs Low groups; plot Kaplan–Meier recurrence-free survival curves with confidence intervals, and perform a log-rank test between the two groups.  

Throughout the process, log key diagnostics: number of matched patients, distribution of proliferation_score, number of events, and any warnings about low sample size or missing data.

Deliverables: 1. A summary of patient ID matching: counts of clinical barcodes, expression-derived barcodes, and their intersection, plus any unmatched IDs.  
2. Proliferation signature mapping report: confirmation of Ensembl IDs found in expression data.  
3. Distribution plot or summary statistics of the proliferation_score.  
4. Cox regression output: table of coefficients, hazard ratios with 95% CI, p-values, and global model fit statistics.  
5. Proportional hazards assumption results, including any variables violating assumptions.  
6. Kaplan–Meier survival curves and log-rank test p-value for high vs low proliferation groups.  
7. A concise write-up of findings: interpretation of the hazard for proliferation_score and implications for recurrence risk.
analysis:
The final analysis was completed successfully. After harmonizing patient barcodes and reducing model complexity, a Cox model was fit on 957 patients (8 events) with covariates: proliferation_score, pharmaceutical therapy, and dichotomized stage (III–IV vs I–II). Results:
– proliferation_score: coef=0.733 (HR=2.08, 95% CI [0.476, 7.96]), p=0.284 (not significant)
– pharmaceutical therapy: coef=4.384 (HR=80.18, 95% CI [10.23, 710.13]), p<0.001 (significant)
– stage_high (III–IV vs I–II): coef=1.770 (HR=5.87, 95% CI [1.22, 28.69]), p=0.029 (significant)
Proportional hazards assumption holds. Kaplan–Meier curves stratified by high vs low proliferation (median split) yielded a log-rank p=0.385, confirming no significant difference in recurrence‐free survival between proliferation groups.
review:
The experiment was mostly implemented as revised: patient IDs were harmonized between expression and clinical data; proliferation scores computed from MKI67, PCNA, and TOP2A; clinical recurrence times and censoring defined correctly; pathologic stages dichotomized; and a parsimonious Cox model fit. Results show proliferation_score HR=2.08 (95% CI 0.48–7.96), p=0.284 (not significant), while pharmaceutical therapy and stage are significant predictors. PH assumptions hold. Therefore, the hypothesis that high proliferation signature predicts shorter time to new tumor event is not supported.  

Minor suggestion: note the limited event count (8 events) and consequent limited power; future studies should increase follow-up or sample size for more robust inference.

Steps: 1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_mutations.csv.
2. Filter clinical to non-missing er_status (Positive or Negative).
3. For each patient, determine mutation status for PIK3CA and TP53 (presence of ≥1 mutation in Hugo_Symbol).
4. Create 2×2 contingency tables for each gene: rows = ER status (Positive, Negative), columns = mutated vs non‐mutated.
5. Perform Fisher’s exact test for each gene.
6. Adjust p-values for two tests using Benjamini–Hochberg.
7. Report odds ratios, confidence intervals, raw p-values, and FDR.
8. Optionally, extend to top 10 most mutated genes beyond PIK3CA/TP53.

Deliverables: • Contingency tables for PIK3CA and TP53.
• Fisher’s test results: odds ratio, 95% CI, raw p-value, FDR.
• Bar plot of mutation frequency by ER status for each gene.
analysis:
The analysis tested whether PIK3CA and TP53 mutation frequencies differ by ER status using Fisher’s exact test (with BH FDR correction). 

PIK3CA:
- ER+ mutated: 302 / (302+506)
- ER− mutated: 34 / (34+204)
- Odds Ratio = 3.581 (95% CI: 2.424–5.289)
- p-value = 2.10×10⁻¹², FDR = 2.10×10⁻¹²

TP53:
- ER+ mutated: 155 / (155+653)
- ER− mutated: 181 / (181+57)
- Odds Ratio = 0.075 (95% CI: 0.053–0.106)
- p-value = 1.61×10⁻⁵⁸, FDR = 3.23×10⁻⁵⁸

Mutation frequency bar plot confirms PIK3CA is enriched in ER+ tumors, while TP53 is enriched in ER− tumors. These differences are highly significant.

hypothesis: Higher HER2 IHC score is associated with increased tumor ERBB2 (HER2) expression.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Assess whether clinical HER2 IHC semi‐quantitative scores correspond to ERBB2 gene expression.

Steps: 1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv.  2. Filter clinical data to patients with non‐missing her2_ihc_score (categories '0','1+','2+','3+').  3. In gene expression, extract ERBB2 row (by Ensembl ID or ‘|ERBB2’).  4. Align barcodes and merge her2_ihc_score with ERBB2 expression.  5. Encode IHC score as ordinal (0=0, 1+=1, 2+=2, 3+=3).  6. Test correlation (Spearman) between score and expression; alternatively, perform Kruskal–Wallis across score groups.  7. Generate boxplot of ERBB2 expression stratified by IHC score.

Deliverables: • Table of group sizes and ERBB2 expression summaries per IHC score.  
• Spearman rho and p‐value (and/or Kruskal–Wallis statistic and p‐value).  
• Boxplot of ERBB2 expression by IHC score.
analysis:
The code correctly loaded clinical and expression data, filtered for non‐missing IHC scores (n=611), extracted ERBB2 expression by Ensembl ID, and merged datasets by patient barcode. Group‐wise ERBB2 expression (mean±SD) was:
• IHC 0 (n=61): 5.74±1.05 (range 2.06–9.18)
• IHC 1+ (n=266): 6.17±0.85 (range 2.30–10.41)
• IHC 2+ (n=196): 6.75±1.16 (range 2.88–10.95)
• IHC 3+ (n=88): 9.14±1.82 (range 4.63–11.93)

Spearman correlation between ordinal IHC score and ERBB2 expression: rho = 0.513, p = 2.7×10⁻⁴². Kruskal–Wallis test across IHC groups: H = 178.0, p = 2.4×10⁻³⁸. Both tests show a highly significant positive association: higher IHC scores correspond to increased ERBB2 transcript levels. The boxplot confirms a stepwise increase in median expression from 0→3+.

analysis:

hypothesis: ERBB2 (HER2) mRNA expression levels are significantly higher in patients with HER2 IHC score 3+ or HER2 FISH positive status compared to those who are IHC 0/1+ and FISH negative.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Test whether HER2 receptor status by IHC/FISH is reflected in ERBB2 transcript levels.

Steps: 1. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv.
2. Filter clinical records to non-missing her2_ihc_score and her2_fish_status.
3. Define two groups: "HER2-positive" (her2_ihc_score == '3+' OR her2_fish_status == 'Positive') and "HER2-negative" (her2_ihc_score in ['0','1+'] AND her2_fish_status == 'Negative').
4. In gene expression data, extract ERBB2 expression using its Ensembl ID (ENSG00000141736).
5. Align patients across clinical and expression datasets.
6. Compare ERBB2 expression between the two groups using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
7. Perform ROC curve analysis to evaluate how well ERBB2 expression discriminates HER2 status; compute AUC.
8. Plot boxplots of ERBB2 expression by group and ROC curve with AUC annotation.

Deliverables: • Counts of patients in each HER2 status group.
• Summary statistics (median, IQR) of ERBB2 expression by group.
• Wilcoxon test statistic and p-value.
• ROC curve plot and AUC value.
• Boxplot of ERBB2 expression by HER2 status.
analysis:
The code successfully loaded clinical and expression data, defined HER2-positive (n=67) and HER2-negative (n=94) groups, and compared ERBB2 expression between them.

Key results:
- HER2-negative: n=94, median ERBB2=6.437 (IQR 5.982–6.931)
- HER2-positive: n=67, median ERBB2=7.837 (IQR 6.947–9.439)
- Mann–Whitney U test: U=5051.0, p<0.0001 (two-sided)
- ROC analysis: AUC=0.802, indicating good discrimination of HER2 status by ERBB2 expression

Box plots show clearly higher ERBB2 levels in HER2-positive patients, and the ROC curve confirms a strong predictive performance (AUC≈0.80).
review:
Hypothesis: ERBB2 mRNA expression levels are higher in patients with HER2 IHC score 3+ or FISH positive status compared to IHC 0/1+ and FISH negative.

Results:
- HER2-positive group (n=67): median ERBB2 expression = 7.837 (IQR 6.947–9.439)
- HER2-negative group (n=94): median ERBB2 expression = 6.437 (IQR 5.982–6.931)
- Mann–Whitney U test: U = 5051.0, p < 0.0001 (two-sided)
- ROC curve analysis: AUC = 0.802, indicating good discrimination of HER2 status by ERBB2 expression.

Findings: The analysis confirms that ERBB2 transcript levels are significantly higher in clinically HER2-positive patients, and ERBB2 expression serves as a reasonably accurate biomarker for HER2 status (AUC≈0.80).

hypothesis: Unsupervised transcriptomic clustering of tumors yields groups whose membership is significantly associated with HER2 IHC score categories.
experiment_plan:
Objective: Cluster patients by global gene expression and test association with HER2 IHC score.

Steps: 1. Load cleaned_gene_expression.csv and cleaned_clinical_data.csv.

Deliverables: Cluster assignments for each patient; chi‐square test p‐value for cluster vs IHC score; PCA scatterplot colored by cluster and IHC category; heatmap of cluster centroids.
analysis:
The clustering analysis was completed successfully.  
• K=3 clusters were fit on the top 2,000 most variable genes reduced via PCA (10 PCs).  
• Cluster assignments were produced for all patients (first 10 shown).  
• The chi‐square test between cluster and HER2 IHC score (0, 1+, 2+, 3+) returned p=0.0146, indicating a significant association.  
• A PCA scatterplot (PC1 vs PC2) shows intermixed IHC scores across the three clusters.  
• A heatmap of cluster centroids in PC space highlights distinct centroid profiles (e.g., Cluster 1 has a strongly negative PC1 centroid).
review:
Hypothesis: Unsupervised clustering of global gene expression into three groups yields clusters whose membership is associated with HER2 IHC score categories.

Implementation: 
- Loaded expression (1068 samples × 60498 genes) and clinical (HER2 IHC scores) data.  
- Selected top 2000 most variable genes, standardized, applied PCA (10 components).  
- Performed K-means (k=3) on PCA scores; merged cluster labels with HER2 IHC scores.  
- Conducted chi-square test on cluster vs IHC categories (0, 1+, 2+, 3+): p=0.0146 (significant association).  
- Generated PCA scatterplot colored by cluster and shaped by IHC score; heatmap of cluster centroids in PC space; printed first 10 cluster assignments.

Findings:  
- Three distinct transcriptomic clusters were identified.  
- Cluster membership is significantly associated with HER2 IHC score (χ² p=0.0146), supporting the hypothesis.  
- PCA plot shows mixed IHC scores across clusters, and centroid heatmap highlights distinct PC profiles per cluster.
